The question of whether humans can live past 150 years is the subject of genuinely conflicting scientific research and expert opinion. Some studies set 150 as an absolute upper ceiling: Gero research found that human body resilience is completely gone between ages 120 and 150, concluding humans "probably can't live longer than 150 years" [d7], and a Nature Communications study similarly found that loss of physiological resilience limits human lives to "120 to 150 years at the most" [d8]. Research published in The Atlantic found that maximum human age plateaued around 115 after 1995, with odds of anyone living past 125 in any given year being less than 1 in 10,000, suggesting the ceiling is "hardwired into our biology" [d6]. On the other side, a University of Georgia researcher argues humans are "not even close" to reaching the maximum potential lifespan, and that longevity records may increase significantly in coming decades [d4]. Dr. Andrew Steele, a computational biologist, states there is "no biological reason humans can't reach the age of 200," and believes someone could reach 150 with the help of drugs currently in human trials [d10]. The longest verified human lifespan remains Jeanne Calment's 122 years and 5 months [d9], and no participant in the GERO.AI study of 70,000 people showed the biological resiliency to live to 150 under current medical conditions [d1][d3].
